statements.text: Saliency-based algorithms can explain the relationship between input image pixels and deep-learning model predictions.

Calibrated confidence reflects the statistical likelihood associated with a model prediction, but it does not constitute a clinical diagnosis or guarantee correctness.
Grad-CAM visualizations highlight influential input regions for a prediction, but they cannot show underlying biological ground truth or prove clinical validation.

summary: Attribution maps highlight regions of an image relevant to deep learning model predictions, but relying solely on visual inspection has limitations. Systematic statistical and quantitative evaluations—such as pixel-intensity correlations, the Pointing Game, and boundary alignment metrics—help bridge visual explainability with objective validation.

statements.text: Attribution maps serve as post-hoc explainability tools that highlight regions of an image most relevant to the predictions made by deep learning models.
Quantitative effectiveness can be explored by employing pixel-intensity correlations, which assess the correlation between saliency map intensity and model accuracy or class probabilities.
The Pointing Game measures correspondence by finding the maximum value of a saliency map and checking its proximity to ground-truth annotations.
Systematic quantitative analysis helps validate the relationship between a saliency method and the model's performance in medical image analysis.

summary: The provided literature discusses class activation maps and deep learning models for identifying disease lesions and regions of interest in medical imaging, specifically on chest radiographs.

statements.text: Class activation maps (CAMs) help identify which parts or pixels of an image have a higher contribution to a particular prediction by highlighting suspicious regions on chest radiographs.
CAM techniques can be applied in CNN models to classify conditions such as COVID-19, pneumonia, and normal chest X-ray images, providing visual explanations for the model's classifications.

summary: Explanation of how model interpretability can guide attention and improve the generalizability of neuroimaging classifiers across multiple cohorts and sites.

statements.text: Deep learning models developed to assess MRI scans face potential variabilities from independent protocols, imaging equipment, radiology artifacts, and demographic shifts.
Domain generalization frameworks have the potential to overcome inter-site and equipment-dependent variabilities by learning transferable signals from source domains to unseen target domains.
Model interpretability can be leveraged to extract disease-relevant information and guide model attention during training to improve generalizability across multiple cohorts.
Attention-based supervision allows models to focus on disease-correlated regions by aligning model attention with class-wise saliency map priors computed over training data.

summary: Deep Bayesian ensemble learning frameworks incorporate uncertainty estimation to help classifiers generalize toward rare and unseen conditions.

statements.text: Real-world medical imaging data often have long-tailed distributions where rare classes are represented by infrequently occurring samples, making it challenging to learn optimal decision boundaries.
Rare classes exhibit higher uncertainties and wider confidence intervals in the prediction space than frequently occurring classes.
By incorporating uncertainty estimates into the model, decision boundaries can be expanded to less frequent classes to help generalize toward rare and unseen conditions.
A deep Bayesian ensemble learning framework with dynamic MC dropout and loss combinations yields better generalization to unseen samples and out-of-distribution detection.

summary: The literature explains that intra-source imbalance in medical datasets introduces training bias and unreliability in deep learning classifiers.

statements.text: Using an intra-source imbalanced dataset causes serious training bias even when the dataset maintains good inter-category balance.
Models trained on intra-source imbalanced datasets can end up classifying images based on data source features rather than pathology, limiting their capability to generalize to other datasets.

summary: The integration of mosaic-based soft labeling and curriculum learning improves the classification performance of tongue lesions in imbalanced datasets.

statements.text: The integration of mosaic-based soft labeling and curriculum learning improves the classification performance of tongue lesions compared to previous methods, establishing a foundation for future research on effectively learning from imbalanced data.
Curriculum learning begins by teaching the model using a simpler training dataset and then gradually introduces more complex data, allowing the model to build on previously learned concepts.

summary: Research explanation regarding dynamic weighting transfer learning for domain shift and class imbalance.

statements.text: Dynamic Weighting Transfer Learning (DTTL) is proposed to address entropy-centric problems and align domain shift in imbalanced medical image classification tasks.
The dynamic transfer learning method measures each medical image according to its imbalance level between two domains.
A balanced translation mechanism generates minority medical images by translating related majority samples, extending decision boundaries among imbalanced classes.
DTTL explores a confidence-based selection method to reserve the most valuable synthesized medical images for further model training.
The Cross-domain Discriminability Adaptation (CDA) and Cross-domain Minority class Translation (CMT) modules play a critical role in addressing domain shift and class imbalance.

summary: This explanation reviews how Generative Adversarial Networks and dual-GAN approaches address class imbalance in brain tumor MRI classification tasks.

statements.text: Generative Adversarial Networks can be leveraged to generate synthetic samples for minority classes, thereby palliating dataset imbalance issues.
Failure to address data imbalance issues in medical imaging datasets may lead to biased results and hinder the model classification process.
Synthetic images generated via GANs can effectively augment training datasets and improve model performance across various tasks.

summary: The literature evaluates ResNet, Swin-Transformer, and MLP-Mixer under distribution shifts in fundus photographs, demonstrating differences in discriminative ability and calibration.

statements.text: Swin-Transformer demonstrated superior and robust discriminative ability compared to ResNet under both in-distribution and distribution shifts in fundus images.
When comparing the discriminative performance across the models under distribution shifts, Swin-Transformer performed the best, followed by ResNet and MLP-Mixer.

MLP-Mixer tended to degrade under distribution shifts caused by Light Transmission Disturbance, whereas both ResNet and Swin-Transformer tended to degrade under distribution shifts caused by Retinal Artifact.

Studies evaluating these architectures did not observe significant differences in calibration ability based on model architecture and size, which is attributed to the unique characteristics of the medical dataset.
